transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

I’m here because I can’t stop noticing this crooked, swollen-looking side of my face in the lesson videos. Once I see it, I just feel like the students, parents, and other staff must be staring at that instead of listening to me.
When you think about how crooked or swollen your face looks, do you feel that this is definitely how others see you, or do you think it's possible you're overestimating how noticeable it really is?
It feels definite to me. When I see that side of my face in the lesson videos, it looks crooked and swollen, and I just assume everyone watching is focused on it instead of what I’m saying.

Aside from your concerns about your face, have you noticed anything else unusual lately—like hearing voices or sounds others don't seem to hear, or having other beliefs that people find hard to accept?
No, I haven’t noticed hearing things that other people don’t hear or anything like that. It’s really just the way my face looks to me.
Do you find yourself repeatedly checking your face in mirrors or camera footage, trying certain angles, or comparing that side of your face to others' faces?

Yes. Before I post a lesson or join a parent conference, I keep changing the camera angle and replaying the clips. I’ll cover part of my face with my hand to see if it looks better, and sometimes I re-record the whole lesson over and over. It takes so long that I miss prep work and end up late for classes.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient demonstrates a preoccupation with a perceived flaw (crooked/swollen side of face) that is not objectively noticeable to the degree perceived, accompanied by repetitive checking and camera/mirror-comparison behaviors, excessive re-recording, and covering the area with her hand. These compulsive appearance-related behaviors cause functional impairment (lateness, missed work prep). She denies hallucinations or other bizarre fixed beliefs, and her preoccupation is limited to appearance, consistent with Body Dysmorphic Disorder. Her conviction is strong ('definite') suggesting absent/poor insight, but the singular focus on appearance without broader delusional system argues against primary psychotic disorder (F22). The repetitive checking is appearance-specific rather than general contamination/order concerns, arguing against OCD (F42.2).

No other unusual or hard-to-accept beliefs reported

additional_requirements: Preoccupation not better explained by eating disorder (no mention of weight/body fat concerns)

Insight appears poor/absent given absolute conviction in perceived defect
